closed.label: Closed book: why models hallucinate your facts

choose.label: RAG vs long context vs fine-tuning

questions.prompt: You ask a model, with no docs in the prompt, for your API's /search limit (100 per minute, written only in your private docs). What does it most likely do?
options: Writes a plausible number, because no weights hold your limit and sampling still picks a token
Returns an error message, because it looks the fact up in its weights and finds no entry for it
Answers 100, because training on many similar API docs placed your exact limit in its weights
Asks for your docs, because a model can always tell which facts it never saw in training
questions.why: The weights hold no path that favours “100”, so probability spreads over plausible numbers (60, 100, 1,000, 10) and sampling picks one. It reads as confidently as a right answer: a hallucination. There is no lookup to fail.

questions.prompt: Putting passage C2 in the prompt made “100” jump to 96%. What changed inside the model?
options: Nothing in the weights: attention read “100” from the passage now in the context
The weights updated to store the new fact, so later questions without C2 also answer 100
Temperature dropped, because a passage in the prompt makes sampling greedy
The vocabulary gained a token for 100, so the model could finally output it
questions.why: The weights are frozen while serving (Lesson 3). The same model, given different context, puts its probability on the token it can read from the passage.

questions.prompt: In RAG, what does the generate stage actually receive?
options: A prompt with instructions, the top k retrieved passages as text, and the question
The passages' embedding vectors, written into the model's weights for the length of one request
The whole docs index, which the model searches itself during its forward pass
Only the question, because retrieval runs after generation to check the answer
questions.why: Retrieve → augment → generate. Retrieval is a separate search system; its output becomes prompt text. Nothing about the model changes.

questions.prompt: With k = 1 the bot answered “10 requests per minute [C3]” to “How often can I call search per minute?”. Where was the bug?
options: Retrieval: C3 (/upload) ranked above C2, so the model answered faithfully from the wrong passage
Generation: the model had C2 in its prompt but copied the wrong number out of that same passage
Chunking: C2 was split at a boundary, so the number 100 was missing from every chunk sent
The model: it ignored the passage it was given and answered from its training data instead
questions.why: Only C3 was sent, and C3 really says 10 (for /upload). The model did its job; retrieval ranked a near-duplicate first. k = 2 includes C2 and the answer becomes 100.

questions.prompt: You raise k from 1 to 3 for the /search question. Select all that are true.
options: The right passage is more likely to be in the prompt
Each question sends more input tokens, so it costs more
The model gets more unrelated text it has to ignore
The model's weights now include the extra passages
Retrieval gets faster, because fewer passages are ranked
questions.why: More passages: more chances to include the right one, more tokens to pay for, more noise. Weights never change, and retrieval still ranks every passage.

questions.prompt: Chunks of 6 words, no overlap: the chunk holding “100” reads “100 requests per minute per API”. Why is that a problem?
options: It lost its subject: no chunk has /search with 100, so a /search question can't match it
It is too long: six words is more than one embedding vector can hold for retrieval
It costs too much: small chunks send more tokens per question than large chunks do
It breaks the index: chunks must share some words, or the index refuses to store them
questions.why: Too small and a fact loses its subject. Overlap or larger chunks keep “/search … 100” together in one chunk.

questions.prompt: What does half overlap between chunks fix?
options: A fact cut at a chunk boundary also appears whole in the neighbouring chunk
Large chunks mix fewer topics, because overlap removes their repeated words
Fewer chunks need storing, because overlapping chunks are merged into one
The question and the chunks can now use two different embedding models
questions.why: Overlap repeats the end of one chunk at the start of the next, so a boundary can't cut every copy of a sentence. The cost is more chunks to store.

questions.prompt: Why is one very large chunk (the whole page) a problem too?
options: Its one vector blends every topic, and each retrieval sends all of that text
The model can't read chunks longer than one sentence, so they get skipped
Large chunks split facts more often, because their boundaries fall in the middle of words
Keyword search stops working, because large chunks contain no rare words
questions.why: A chunk gets one vector, so many topics blur into it and it matches none sharply; and you pay k × chunk size in tokens per question.

questions.prompt: Your docs are 50K tokens and change rarely. The context window is 128K. What's the simplest good choice?
options: Paste all the docs into the prompt; prompt caching cuts the repeated cost
Fine-tune on the docs, because facts in the weights cost no input tokens
Build RAG, because a long prompt can never show which passage it used
None works, because 50K tokens is over the model's context window limit
questions.why: It fits, so long context is simplest. RAG wins once the docs outgrow the window or the per-question bill. Fine-tuning is unreliable for exact facts.

questions.prompt: Your docs are 2M tokens and edited daily. Which approach fits?
options: RAG: about 1,000 input tokens per question, and edits show up once changed chunks are re-embedded
Long context: paste everything, because a bigger prompt always gives the model more facts to use
Fine-tuning: retrain daily, because the weights are the most reliable place to keep exact facts
Raise k until it covers every chunk, because recall@k reaches 100% only when all chunks are sent
questions.why: 2M tokens can't fit a 128K window. Fine-tuning needs a training run per edit and can't cite. RAG's cost is k × chunk size whatever the docs size.

questions.prompt: Why is fine-tuning a poor way to add facts the bot must quote exactly?
options: Each edit needs a training run, and the model can't point to where a fact came from
Fine-tuning erases the model's earlier training, so it forgets how to write sentences
A fine-tuned model needs a longer context window for every question it is asked
Fine-tuning only changes the tokenizer, so the new facts never reach the weights
questions.why: Fine-tuning changes behaviour (tone, format, a narrow task) well. For facts that change and must be checkable, it is slow to update and gives no source.

questions.prompt: You paste 50,000 tokens of docs into every question, at $3 per million input tokens. What does one question cost, in dollars?
questions.why: 50,000 × $3 / 1,000,000 = $0.15 per question. Sending the 3 best passages (~1,000 tokens) costs $0.003: 50× less.

questions.prompt: In vector search, what is embedded ahead of time, and what at ask time?
options: Every chunk ahead of time (the index); the question at ask time
The question ahead of time; every chunk at ask time, to stay fresh
Both at ask time, because each chunk's vector depends on the question
Nothing ahead of time; the model embeds the docs during its prefill
questions.why: Indexing embeds each chunk once. Each question costs one embedding call plus a similarity score per stored vector.

questions.prompt: Why must the question and the chunks go through the same embedding model?
options: Vectors from different models live in unrelated spaces, so their cosine means nothing
Different models cut the docs into different chunks, so their ranks can't be compared
The context window only accepts vectors made by the model that writes the answer
Keyword scores are computed from the embedding model's vocabulary of rare words
questions.why: Directions only mean something within one model's space. Swapping the embedding model means re-embedding every chunk.

questions.prompt: Cosine similarity between a question and a passage measures…
options: How closely their embedding vectors point in the same direction
How many exact words the question and the passage have in common
How long the passage is compared with the length of the question
How likely the model is to generate the passage as its next text
questions.why: Cosine = dot product ÷ both lengths: direction only (Lesson 1). Shared exact words is keyword search.

questions.prompt: “What does E1042 mean?” Vector search ranks the 429 passage first. Why does keyword search find C6?
options: Only C6 contains the exact token E1042, a rare word that keyword scoring rewards
Keyword search gives E1042 a longer vector, so its cosine with C6 comes out higher
Keyword search ranks passages by their length, and C6 is the shortest passage
Keyword search knows E1042 is an error code, so it ranks error passages first
questions.why: Rare exact codes are keyword search's best case. Vector search sees “some error” and blurs E1042 into the 429 passage.

questions.prompt: “How often can I call search per minute?” Which method on its own matches “call” to “requests”?
options: Vector search, because similar meanings get similar embeddings
Keyword search, because both words appear somewhere in the docs
Neither one, because only an LLM judge can match two synonyms
Keyword search, because rarer words count more in its scoring
questions.why: Keyword search needs the same word; vector search matches meaning. Hybrid runs both and merges the rankings.

questions.prompt: Reciprocal rank fusion adds 1/(60 + rank) from each list. A passage is rank 2 in vector search and rank 1 in keyword search. What is its hybrid score?
questions.why: 1/62 + 1/61 = 0.0161 + 0.0164 = 0.0325. That is C2 for the /search question, just above C3 (1/61 + 1/63 = 0.0323).

questions.prompt: Exact search over 100 million vectors of 1,024 numbers each. About how many multiply-adds per question, in billions?
questions.why: 100,000,000 × 1,024 ≈ 102 billion (≈ 100 billion), for every question. An approximate index checks only a few percent of that.

questions.prompt: An approximate index checks only the regions nearest the question. What does it give up for the speed?
options: Recall: a true nearest neighbour in an unchecked region can be missed
Freshness: a newly added vector can't be found until the next full rebuild
Cost: every approximate search adds extra input tokens to the prompt
Precision: the cosine scores it returns are rounded, so ties appear
questions.why: Checking fewer regions = fewer vectors compared = faster, at the cost of sometimes missing a true neighbour. The regions-checked knob sets the trade.

questions.prompt: In the regions toy, the question sits near a region border. Checking 1 of 16 regions finds only 1 of the 5 true nearest. Why?
options: Some true neighbours sit in nearby regions that weren't checked
One region holds fewer than 5 vectors, so it can't return 5 results
The question's vector moves when fewer regions are being checked
Inside each region, the index ranks vectors by keyword score instead
questions.why: Near a border, neighbours spill into adjacent regions. Checking 4 regions (100 of 400 vectors) finds all 5.

questions.prompt: “Do you support GraphQL?” is not in the docs. With no score floor, what does the bot do?
options: Answers from the nearest passages anyway, because top-k always returns k results
Says it's not in the docs, because cosine is negative for every unrelated passage
Returns no passages, because vector search only ever returns exact word matches
Fails with an error, because the prompt then has no passage it is able to cite
questions.why: There is always a nearest neighbour, however far away. The bot gets three unrelated passages (best 0.41) and answers a different question.

questions.prompt: You raise the floor to 0.90. For the /search question, the best passage scores 0.86. What happens?
options: Every passage is dropped, so an answerable question gets “not in the docs”
Only C2 passes, because a high floor removes near-duplicate passages such as C3
Nothing changes, because the floor only applies to off-topic questions
The bot answers 10, because C3 is the one passage above the floor
questions.why: Too high and the floor refuses real questions; too low and it lets unrelated passages through. 0.50 works for both questions here.

questions.prompt: How should you choose the score floor's value?
options: Tune it on test questions, including some whose right answer is “not in the docs”
Use 0.50 always, because cosine values are the same across embedding models
Set it to the highest score seen, so only the very best passage ever passes
Set it to 0, because the model ignores irrelevant passages in the prompt anyway
questions.why: Cosine ranges depend on the embedding model, so there's no universal floor. And models are easily distracted by irrelevant text.

questions.prompt: Right-passage ranks for six golden questions are 2, 1, 2, 3, 1, 1. What is recall@2, in percent?
questions.why: Ranks ≤ 2: five of six questions. 5/6 = 83%.

questions.prompt: Same ranks: 2, 1, 2, 3, 1, 1. What is recall@1, in percent?
questions.why: Ranks = 1: three of six. 3/6 = 50%.

questions.prompt: Why keep a golden set instead of trying a few questions by hand after each change?
options: The same questions with known answers every run, so scores compare and regressions show
Hand checks rely on the LLM judge, which disagrees with human labels far too often
A golden set makes retrieval itself faster, because the right answers get cached
The similarity score already shows whether an answer is right, so hand checks add nothing
questions.why: Hand checks vary and skip questions that used to work. A similarity score says how close a passage is, not whether it answers the question.

questions.prompt: What does computing recall@k need?
options: For each question, which passage is right and where it ranked
A person reading and grading every single answer the bot writes
An LLM judge scoring each answer against a written rubric
The model's probability for every token of each answer
questions.why: Recall@k needs no model to grade: it's a lookup of where the right passage ranked.

questions.prompt: G6: the right passage (24 hours) was retrieved, but the bot said 48 hours. What kind of miss, and what fixes it?
options: An answer miss: fix the prompt or the model, since a bigger k can't help
A retrieval miss: raise k so that more of the ranked passages reach the prompt
A chunking miss: add overlap so the passage keeps its subject
A grading miss: the judge misread an answer that was correct
questions.why: The passage arrived, so retrieval worked. A strict prompt (answer only from the passages, quote them) fixed it in the lesson.

questions.prompt: With k = 1 the bot answered “10” from C3, which really says 10. Is that answer faithful, and is it right?
options: Faithful but wrong: it stuck to its passage, but retrieval sent the wrong one
Unfaithful and wrong: it changed the number given in the passage it read
Faithful and right: it cited the passage it was given, so it is correct
Unfaithful but right: the model corrected a mistake in the passage
questions.why: Faithful = sticks to the passages it was given. That's why retrieval and generation are scored separately.

questions.prompt: Plain prompt, k = 1 → k = 3 on the golden set. Select all that are true.
options: Retrieval misses drop from 3 to 0
Right answers rise from 2 to 5
G6's answer miss disappears
End-to-end accuracy reaches 100%
questions.why: A bigger k fixes retrieval misses only. G6 had its passage all along, so it stays wrong until the prompt changes: 5 of 6.

questions.prompt: Reference: “100 requests per minute per API key”. Why does exact match fail “100 requests per minute.”?
options: It compares strings, so a right answer worded differently fails
It compares meanings, and the final period changes the meaning
It fails any answer shorter than the reference, right or wrong
It applies the judge's rubric, which requires the words API key
questions.why: Exact match suits short, fixed outputs (like a passage ID). Free-text answers need a grader that accepts paraphrases.

questions.prompt: The plain LLM judge passed “Limits vary by endpoint and plan; check your dashboard…”. What made it match the human label?
options: A rubric that says passing means stating 100 requests per minute for /search
Switching to exact match, because exact match never passes long answers
Raising k, so that the judge sees more of the retrieved passages
A bigger judge model, because only small judges show verbosity bias
questions.why: Judges favour fluent, longer answers (verbosity bias). A rubric says what passing means; with it the judge matched all 5 human labels.

questions.prompt: How do you know an LLM judge can be trusted?
options: Measure its agreement with human labels on a sample; fix the rubric until it's high
It is a model too, so its grades are as accurate as the answers it is grading
Check that it passes longer, more detailed answers more often than short ones
Run it twice on the same answers; if both sets of grades match, the grades are correct
questions.why: A judge is trusted only as far as it agrees with people. Strong judges reach over 80% agreement, about the level between two humans.

questions.prompt: Today: vector search, k = 3, recall 100%, 1,000 tokens per question. Gate: recall ≥ today and tokens ≤ today. Which change ships?
options: Hybrid search with k = 2: recall 100% with 700 tokens
Hybrid search with k = 1: recall 83% with 400 tokens
Vector search with k = 2: recall 83% with 700 tokens
Vector search with k = 4: recall 100% with 1,300 tokens
questions.why: Only hybrid k = 2 keeps recall and lowers tokens: 30% cheaper at the same quality.

questions.prompt: Each question sends 100 tokens of instructions and question, plus k passages of 300 tokens. How many input tokens at k = 2?
Hybrid search raises recall@1 from 50% to 83%. Why still read the per-question list?
options: An aggregate can hide a regression: G2 fell from #1 to #2 under hybrid
Recall@1 is computed per question, so the aggregate is always wrong
Hybrid scores use a different scale, so the two recall percentages don't compare
The golden set's questions change whenever the search method changes
questions.why: Hybrid helped G1, G3 and G4 but pushed G2 down (keyword search ranked it last of four passages containing “API”). Good reports list which questions changed.
